dossier.public_summary: The dip seen in two sectors disappears in a third and individual transits vary by an order of magnitude, so it is not consistent, repeatable transits. With no clear sky location and a nearby star able to mimic the dip, a blended eclipsing binary is a better explanation than a planet.

reasons.why: Depth is not steady. sector_depths_by_source verdict is changes_within_a_source (p_constant_all=5.584886829711268e-17) even though each source is formally steady, so the change is intrinsic, not a calibration offset.
reasons.value: p_constant=5.286e-17 depth_change_pct=170.9 per_sector [7:4006 ppm, 33:1909 ppm, 87:406 ppm]

reasons.why: Individual transits are inconsistent. Two sectors (7 and 33) give deep dips while the third sector (87) shows no dip, so the signal is driven by a few outlier events, not repeatable transits.
reasons.value: p_consistent=1.5868335027842584e-17 share_of_top_3=0.991 outliers: 4595 ppm (5.2 sigma), 3692 ppm (4.5 sigma), 404 ppm (-4.4 sigma), 408 ppm (-4.4 sigma)

reasons.why: No on-target centroid to rule out a blended neighbour within one TESS pixel, and a plausible contaminant exists that could cause the 2134 ppm dip with a ~4.7% eclipse.
reasons.value: verdict=inconclusive why=no sector with a clear difference image neighbours plausible_within_1px=1 could_cause_within_1px=2 closest_that_could 2.5 arcsec 3.35 mag 0.0466

reasons.why: Very low planet-like rank supports the false-positive interpretation. Size (rp_rearth=2.981) and flat shape (v_sigma=-3.133) plus no odd_even diff (0.6072) or secondary (3.036) would favour a planet, but they are outweighed by the strong variability evidence.
